title: How to write a business proposal email that gets results
summary: Learn how to write a business proposal email that gets opened, read, and answered, with structure, examples, and subject line tips included.
body_markdown:
You've spent hours nailing the scope and price, but if your business proposal email lands with a vague subject line and a wall of text, it may go unread. Learning how to write a business proposal email that gets results starts before you type a single word, with research into what your prospect actually needs, and it ends with a clear, single next step that makes replying easy. In between, the right subject line, a personalized opening, and a tight summary of your solution do the work of turning a cold pitch into a signed deal. This guide walks through each phase of that email, from the first line to the follow-up message you send if you hear nothing back. For a broader look at proposal strategy beyond the email itself, check out our complete guide to business proposals.

## Do your research before you write the email


An effective way to write a business proposal email that gets results is to research the recipient before drafting a single line. A few minutes of prep tells you who should receive the email, what problem to lead with, and which details will make your pitch feel specific instead of generic. Skipping this step is why so many proposal emails read like templates and get ignored.


Start by identifying the actual decision-maker and their role, not just the person who first replied to your inquiry. Note any pain points or goals they mentioned in earlier calls or emails, and check the company's website or recent news for a detail worth referencing. If you want a broader walkthrough of this prep work, our step-by-step guide for freelancers covers it in more depth.


## Write a subject line that gets opened


A proposal email's subject line decides whether the message gets opened or buried, so keep it under eight words and specific to the project you're pitching. "Business proposal" or "Following up" tell the reader nothing and often get skipped in a crowded inbox. Instead, reference the exact work or a prior conversation so the recipient quickly knows why you're writing.


- **Project-specific:** "Proposal for \[Company\]'s website redesign"
- **Referral-based:** "Referred by \[Name\]: social media proposal"
- **Conversation callback:** "Following up on our call about \[project\]"
- **Outcome-focused:** "A plan to cut your onboarding time"


Each version signals relevance in the first glance, which is often the only chance a subject line gets.


## Open with a personalized greeting and hook


Once the subject line earns the open, the first two sentences decide whether the recipient keeps reading. Start with the recipient's actual name, rather than a generic "Dear Sir or Madam" or "To whom it may concern," since those greetings signal a mass email. Follow the name with a one-line reference to how the conversation started, whether that's a referral, a discovery call, or an inbound inquiry, so the reader quickly places the context.


From there, get to the point fast. A freelance copywriter emailing a bakery owner after a referral might open with: "Hi Maria, Josh mentioned you're looking to refresh your website copy before the spring menu launch." That single line proves you listened and sets up the message that follows.


## Introduce your business and the problem you solve


After the hook, resist the urge to paste in your full company bio. Keep the introduction to one or two sentences, and use it to name the specific problem the client is facing rather than list out the services you offer. A copywriter emailing that bakery owner might write: "I'm a copywriter who helps small food businesses turn seasonal menu changes into website updates that don't sit in a queue for weeks." That single sentence names the problem (slow website updates around launches) and positions the writer as the person who solves it.


Connect your experience directly to the problem instead of general credentials. Mention a similar client or project only if it reinforces that you've solved this exact issue before. For more on structuring this part of the message, see our guide on business proposal format for success.

## Present your solution, scope, and price


The body of your business proposal email should summarize your solution in a few lines, not restate the entire proposal. Once you've named the client's problem, follow with a short list of what you'll deliver so the reader can scan the scope quickly.


- **Deliverable:** Homepage and menu-page copy refresh
- **Timeline:** Two weeks from kickoff to final draft
- **Investment:** Around $1,800, detailed in the attached proposal


Mention the price range briefly instead of a full cost breakdown. A specific number or range builds trust, while a long list of line items belongs in the attached document. Close this section by pointing to the full proposal: "I've attached the full proposal with a detailed breakdown of the work and pricing." That line keeps the email skimmable while giving the client an easy path to the details when they're ready to dig in.


## End with one clear call to action


A business proposal email should close with one clear request, not a scattered list of options. Asking a client to "reply, schedule a call, or let me know if you have questions" forces them to choose, and most readers default to doing nothing. Pick the single next step that actually moves the deal forward, whether that's a reply confirming interest, a scheduled call, or a signature on the attached agreement.


Make that step easy to act on. Suggest two specific times for a call instead of asking "when works for you," or include a scheduling link so the recipient can pick a slot without an email back-and-forth. For more phrasing examples, see our proposal letter tips and examples.


## Proofread, format, and follow up


Before you hit send, read the email once for content and once for format. A proposal email with the right numbers but a wall of unbroken text loses readers just as fast as one with typos, since most people scan client emails on a phone screen between meetings.


Keep paragraphs to two or three sentences and add a blank line between each one. Double-check the client's name, company name, and each figure in the email against the attached proposal. A price that doesn't match between the email and the document raises doubt before the client has even reviewed the work.


If you don't hear back, send one polite follow-up after three to five business days rather than repeated check-ins. A short note like "Wanted to make sure this landed in your inbox, happy to answer any questions" keeps the tone warm without pressuring the reader toward a decision.

## FAQ


### **Q1: How do you write a business proposal email that gets a response?**


A business proposal email gets a response when it opens with a subject line specific to the project, greets the recipient by name, and states one clear problem you can solve for them. Keep the body short: a one-line hook, a brief statement of the problem, a quick summary of the solution and price, and a single call to action. Emails that ask for one specific next step, like confirming a call time, get replies more often than emails that list multiple vague options.


Research also plays a big role in response rates. Referencing a detail from a prior call or a specific pain point the recipient mentioned shows the email was written for them, not copied from a template. A freelance copywriter who opens with a bakery owner's actual spring launch deadline, for example, signals relevance in the first sentence and gives the reader a reason to keep reading.


### **Q2: What should you include in a proposal email to a client?**


A proposal email to a client should include a personalized greeting, a one-line hook tied to their situation, a short statement of the problem you solve, a brief summary of your proposed solution and price range, and one clear call to action. The full scope, detailed pricing, and terms belong in an attached or linked proposal document, not in the email body itself.


Think of the email as a preview that earns a click, not the pitch itself. A short deliverables list with three or four items, like the timeline and investment range, gives the reader enough to gauge interest before they open the attachment. Closing with a line like "I've attached the full proposal with a detailed breakdown" keeps the email skimmable while pointing to where the details live.


### **Q3: What's a good subject line for a business proposal email?**


A good subject line for a business proposal email is under eight words and references the specific project, referral, or prior conversation instead of a generic phrase like "Business proposal" or "Following up." Examples include "Proposal for \[Company\]'s website redesign" or "Referred by \[Name\]: social media proposal." Specificity signals relevance in the split second before a recipient decides whether to open an email.


Outcome-focused subject lines can also work well, especially when the recipient hasn't spoken with you directly yet. A line like "A plan to cut your onboarding time" names a benefit rather than a deliverable, which can catch attention in a crowded inbox. Whichever format you choose, avoid vague or overly broad subject lines that could apply to any recipient.


### **Q4: How long should a business proposal email be?**


A business proposal email should run about 150 to 250 words, short enough to read on a phone screen between meetings. That length is enough room for a personalized hook, a one- or two-sentence problem statement, a brief solution and price summary, and a single call to action, without repeating what's already covered in the attached proposal document.


Longer emails tend to lose readers before they reach the actual request. Breaking the email into short paragraphs of two or three sentences, with a blank line between each, makes even a slightly longer message easier to scan. If the email starts running past a few short paragraphs, that's usually a sign some of that detail belongs in the attached proposal instead.


### **Q5: How does Bonsai help with business proposal emails?**

Bonsai CRM also stores deal stages, notes, and client history in one record, which makes it faster to pull up the specific detail worth referencing in a proposal email's opening line. If a discovery call happened over Zoom, the meeting transcript can sync to that same client record, putting the exact pain point a client mentioned within easy reach before the next email goes out.


A business proposal email tends to work well when it's built in layers: research that earns a personal opening line, a subject line and hook that get it read, and a scope and price summary tight enough to skim before the reader ever opens the attachment. Close with one clear ask instead of several vague ones, and the reply you get back is far more likely to move the deal forward. Tools like Bonsai proposals and CRM can help keep that research, tracking, and follow-up organized as your pipeline grows, so each new email starts from real context instead of a blank page.
